title: CFA Ethics 19: Standard I(C) - plagiarism, attribution and AI-generated content
subtitle: Misrepresentation does not need an intent to deceive before it becomes a violation
whyItMatters: This is the standard that AI tools have just made considerably harder: copying no longer leaves an obvious trace, and the line between 'consulting a source' and 'taking it as your own' has blurred. The rule has not changed, but the number of times a day you have to apply it has jumped.
openingQuestion: You use a language model to draft the industry overview section of your report, then edit it in places. Under Standard I(C), is there a problem?
openingOptions: No, because you edited it afterwards, so it is your own work
Yes, if the reader understands it to be your own analysis
No, because an AI tool is not a copyright-holding author
Yes, Standard I(C) bans the use of AI tools in analysis outright
explanation: Standard I(C) has two limbs and both are touched here. The first is misattribution: presenting someone else's work - or a tool's - as your own is misrepresentation, even where nobody suffers financial harm. The second limb weighs more heavily on the analyst's craft: content generated by a language model can contain fabricated figures that look entirely convincing, so putting it into a report without verification means putting in assertions you have no basis for. CFA Institute does not forbid the use of the tools; it requires you to take responsibility for every word that carries your name.

summary.keyIdea: This standard protects the READER rather than measuring the writer's motive, so from its point of view the damage done by carelessness and by deliberate conduct is the same.
summary.commonMistake: Assuming AI-generated content needs no attribution because it has no author. Responsibility for accuracy still belongs to whoever signs their name under the report.

application.title: A rule you can actually use
application.message: If a sentence is not something you worked out and not a fact everyone knows, it needs a source - even when you have rewritten it in your own words.

sections.text: Standard I(C) prohibits every form of misrepresentation, and in analytical work it touches three very ordinary things: quotation, plagiarism, and now content generated by AI tools.
Two limbs of the same standard

The first limb is misattribution: presenting someone else's work - or a tool's - as your own is misrepresentation, even where nobody suffers financial harm and even where it was only carelessness. No intent to deceive is needed to constitute a violation.

left.label: No attribution needed
left.text: Widely published facts: macroeconomic data, closing prices, the contents of financial statements already in the public domain.

right.label: Attribution required
right.text: Someone else's interpretation, forecast, model and conclusions - that is, the part with intellectual work inside it.

sections.text: CFA Institute does not forbid the use of the tools; it requires you to take responsibility for every word that carries your name. The heavier problem for an analyst is that a language model can produce fabricated figures that look entirely convincing - putting them into a report without verification means making assertions with no basis, and that touches Standard V(A) as well.

sections.label: A common misunderstanding
sections.text: The firm owning a document does not make you its author. Reusing a report written by a former colleague and putting your own name on it is still a violation.
Four everyday situations, three of which are violations

sections.title: The boundary of the duty to attribute
sections.subtitle: No intent to deceive is needed - only a reader who is left wrong about who produced that part

concepts.def: Widely acknowledged factual data falls within the exception. Nobody is going to think you measured inflation yourself.
Rephrasing does not make it yours. This is someone else's judgement, and the reader is weighing it as though it were yours.
The firm owning a document does not make you its author. This is the most common misunderstanding and also the easiest kind to detect.

Not prohibited, but you are responsible for every word. If the tool invents a quotation or a figure and you do not check it, that is a misrepresentation carrying your name - the fact that a machine produced it is not a mitigating circumstance.

sections.label: Why the second limb is more dangerous than the plagiarism one
sections.text: Misrepresentation is not only claiming credit for someone else's work; it also covers overstating your own capabilities or your firm's - promising a level of return, describing a risk management process as tighter than it really is, or letting a client believe you have expertise in an area you have never worked in. This limb needs no intent to deceive and no harm to anyone: the measure is whether the reader understood correctly, not whether you meant to leave them wrong.

lines: Attributing a source does not make you smaller.
It is the only thing that makes the rest of the report worth believing.

realWorldExample.company: The exception for published factual data
realWorldExample.description: Standard I(C) does not require a citation for facts already widely published - exchange rates, policy interest rates, official statistics. The boundary sits here: facts no, but someone else's analysis, forecast, classification and interpretation yes. Copying a table of GDP figures needs no attribution; copying the way an economist divides the cycle into phases and explains what caused them does.

quiz.question: Does a Standard I(C) violation require an intent to deceive?
options: No, but it applies only to material published outside the firm
Yes, you must prove the writer deliberately misled the reader
Yes, and actual financial harm to the client has to accompany it
No, careless attribution on its own is enough for a violation
quiz.explanation: This is where the standard is strict: the test is the misleading result, not the writer's state of mind. Requiring proof of deliberate intent would make the standard almost unenforceable, since intent lives in someone's head. Requiring financial harm would leave a false claim untouched until a client happened to lose money on it. And the standard is not limited to external publications - an internal memo that misattributes work misleads its readers just as effectively.

quiz.question: Which case does NOT require attribution?
options: Widely published factual data such as the policy interest rate
One economist's particular way of dividing the business cycle
A growth forecast published recently by an outside research house
A valuation model built by a colleague inside your own firm
quiz.explanation: The boundary runs between facts and interpretation. The number belongs to everyone; the way it is arranged and explained belongs to whoever thought of it. A way of dividing the cycle is a classification someone constructed, a growth forecast is a judgement about the future, and a colleague's valuation model is intellectual work regardless of the firm owning the file it sits in. All three carry a duty to attribute.

quiz.question: What is the particular risk of putting language-model output into a report?
options: The AI tool retains copyright over all the text it generates
The output can contain fabricated figures that look convincing
Regulators forbid the use of AI tools in investment analysis
AI-written text always runs longer than a report requires
quiz.explanation: This is where Standard I(C) meets Standard V(A): an assertion you cannot verify is an assertion with no reasonable basis. Copyright is a legal question about ownership rather than the accuracy problem the standard cares about. Regulators have not banned these tools, and neither has CFA Institute. Length is a matter of editing, and trimming an over-long passage does nothing at all about a figure inside it that was invented.

quiz.question: What is writing on a CV that you are 'a Level II candidate' before passing Level I?
options: A problem only if the employer relied on that in its decision
An acceptable phrasing, since you really are studying that material
A Standard I(C) violation: misstating professional qualifications
A Standard IV violation, since it concerns the employer relation
quiz.explanation: Professional qualifications fall within Standard I(C) alongside experience and investment results, and CFA Institute treats this group of violations very seriously. Whether the employer relied on the statement is irrelevant, because the standard measures the misleading claim rather than its consequences. Studying the material genuinely does not make the description accurate. And Standard IV concerns duties to an employer you already have, not claims made to a prospective one.

quiz.question: How should reusing a colleague's report inside the same firm be handled?
options: Attribution is needed only when the report leaves the firm
Not needed, as internal material belongs to the whole firm
Not needed if the colleague agreed to the reuse verbally beforehand
You must still make clear which parts are someone else's work
quiz.explanation: The firm's ownership of a document and the duty to attribute work correctly are two different things. The firm owning the document does not make you its author. A colleague's verbal agreement cannot waive that either, because the duty runs to the reader rather than to the colleague. And confining the duty to external reports would mean an internal reader is entitled to a wrong impression of who did the work.

keyTakeaways: No intent to deceive is needed - careless attribution is still a violation
Widely published facts need no source; interpretation and forecasts do
AI-generated content: take responsibility for every word carrying your name
An unverifiable figure is an assertion with no basis - it touches Standard V(A) too
The firm owning a document does not make you its author

practicePrompt.question: You quote a passage of another institution's analysis in your report, fully attributed, but drop the risk warning that accompanied it in the original. How should this be assessed?
options: Valid, since the source was fully and properly attributed in the report
Still misrepresentation: selective quotation changes the meaning
A problem only if the other institution objects to the quotation
Valid if you add a risk warning of your own alongside the passage
practicePrompt.explanation: Attribution deals with the misattribution limb, not with the misleading limb. A quotation that is accurate word for word can still create an impression that is the opposite of the original once the qualifying conditions are cut away - and the reader believes they are seeing the quoted party's complete view.
